honesty.seal: Everything you see runs in your browser; the hash and the signature are real and computed locally with Web Crypto. There is no server.
hero.lead: An audit log looks the same after someone deletes a row. The only way to know what happened is to make every entry cryptographically depend on the one before it.
hero.figure.label: A six-link chain with its hashes. The fourth link was altered and its hash changed, so the fifth and sixth links are invalid: they still point at the old hash.
hero.figure.caption: Link 4 was rewritten and its hash recomputed. Links 5 and 6 still point at the previous hash, so the break propagates forward.
hero.note: The prefixes you see are the first characters of real SHA-256, computed in this browser over each record's canonical bytes. Hover a link to read the full hash.
problem.lead: Below is an access log over medical records. Someone with write access deleted one row and edited one cell. The database still answers queries and flags nothing: the log looks spotless.
problem.log.caption: Access log · North Hospital · 2 March 2026
problem.reveal.hide: Show the log as it stands
problem.reveal.aria: Reveal or hide the evidence of the deletion and the edit
problem.summary.intact: The system shows 6 accesses. No query fails. Nothing suggests anything is missing.
problem.summary.revealed: The evidence says 7 accesses: the 11:47 one is missing, and the 10:41 row says “read” where it said “export”.
problem.finding.deleted: Deleted row: the 11:47 access from soporte.externo@vendor is no longer in the table.
problem.finding.modified: Rewritten cell: the 10:41 action went from “export” to “read”, while the user and the record were left untouched.
problem.finding.point: Both tables look identical. That is the problem: without a hash chain there is no way to tell evidence from fiction, and the log gives nothing away.
problem.finding.contrast: With a hash chain, that edit and that deletion break the chaining at exactly those two rows, and verification shows it unambiguously.
idea.lead: A hash chain turns a list into evidence. Each entry is hashed together with the previous entry's hash, so changing any entry changes its hash and, with it, the hash of every entry after it.
idea.entry.label: Entry
idea.preimage.title: The preimage that gets hashed
idea.preimage.note: The engine serializes these three fields into canonical bytes — you can see them below — and runs SHA-256 over those bytes. The “previous hash” field is what makes every entry depend on the whole history.
idea.note.label: Entries recomputed downstream:
idea.count.label: Entries in the chain:
idea.seed.note: The first two entries are plain text and you can edit them: change one and watch the hashes of every entry after it get rewritten.
idea.limit.note: Here the preimage has three fields so it fits on screen. A real system also includes actor, action, resource and timestamp; the mechanism is exactly the same.
idea.next: In block 5 you will break a chain on purpose and watch verification fail at the exact row.
comparison.lead: Four ways to protect an audit log. The useful question is not which one is strongest, but what each one proves and at what cost.
comparison.table.caption: What each option proves, what it does not prevent, and what it costs to run.
comparison.row.chain: Hash chain (the recommended option for an audit log)
comparison.cell.permissions.proves: Who may write. Nothing about what was written.
comparison.cell.permissions.blind: The database administrator, anyone with write access, and a silent UPDATE: the log stays just as believable.
comparison.cell.permissions.keys: Accounts and passwords, which have to be rotated and audited separately.
comparison.cell.permissions.cost: Almost zero: you already have it.
comparison.cell.permissions.complexity: Low. It is the default state of any database.
comparison.cell.signatures.proves: Who issued each record and that it was not changed afterwards, as long as you trust that key and it is still valid.
comparison.cell.signatures.blind: The issuer: whoever signs can rewrite their own record and sign again. It does not prevent deleting whole records or reordering them either.
comparison.cell.signatures.keys: One private key per issuer, with custody and revocation. That is the hardest part to operate.
comparison.cell.signatures.cost: One signature per record: more CPU on write and more bytes per row.
comparison.cell.signatures.complexity: Medium. Verification means managing key lifecycles.
comparison.cell.chain.proves: That nobody edited, deleted, reinserted or reordered an entry without breaking the chain, since the last anchored root.
comparison.cell.chain.blind: Cutting the tail: deleting the last entries leaves a valid but shorter chain. That is why the root is published and signed every N entries; without anchoring, tampering never expires.
comparison.cell.chain.keys: Only for anchoring and signed export; the chain itself needs no keys.
comparison.cell.chain.cost: One SHA-256 per entry. Verifying 10,000 entries takes milliseconds.
comparison.cell.chain.complexity: Low: one hash field per row and the discipline of never rewriting backwards.
comparison.cell.blockchain.proves: The same as the chain plus agreed ordering between organisations that do not trust each other.
comparison.cell.blockchain.blind: Nothing extra for a single organisation: with no extra cryptography it still depends on who controls the nodes.
comparison.cell.blockchain.keys: Wallets, nodes and contracts: a much wider key-custody surface.
comparison.cell.blockchain.cost: High: writes, consensus, infrastructure and energy.
comparison.cell.blockchain.complexity: High. Worth it only when several parties do not trust each other.
comparison.footnote: A practical rule: permissions decide who writes, the hash chain proves what was written, and signed anchoring proves when. Blockchain only when several organisations that do not trust each other share the log.
